A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fourier-based regression work by the same authors. Their main text, figures, equations and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite the changed title, algorithm name and formatting.

before.justification: Section 7 and Figures 2–3 report original audio-signal regression experiments, including prediction errors, confidence regions and running times.

after.justification: Section 7 retains the original audio-signal experiments and their prediction, error and timing results in Figures 2–3.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains its core procedure under the name DUPA instead of PADUA. However, Appendix G adds Generalized DUPA: it queries outside the target domain, weights observations using a smooth cutoff and restricts predictions back to the target domain. This replaces v1's informal non-periodic boundary-correction suggestion with a proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate regression on segments of the same Houdini audio recording. The non-periodic extension and reinforcement-learning motivation in v2 introduce no additional evaluated datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: The experimentally evaluated comparators remain Nadaraya–Watson and Local Polynomial Estimators. Although v2 adds kernel ridge regression to the analytical complexity comparison in Table 1, Section 7 explicitly excludes it from the experiment.

E3.justification: Both versions retain separate tuning and testing segments, Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.1, sample sizes 100, 200, 500 and 1000, approximately 550 prediction points, and supremum-error/runtime evaluation. Renaming the design from active sampling to passive design does not change its stated non-adaptive operation.

E4.justification: The audio reconstruction illustration and error/runtime analyses are retained. No new ablation, robustness test or supplementary empirical analysis evaluates the Bernstein or non-periodic extensions.

E5.justification: Figure 3 reports averaging over five random seeds and 95% confidence intervals in both versions; Figure 2 retains its 95% confidence regions. The new Bernstein inequalities concern theoretical guarantees rather than experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 retain the same prediction curves, error trends and timing results after the algorithm rename. The reported findings—accuracy comparable to NW, faster error reduction than LPE and lower running time—remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds bounded-noise assumptions, Bernstein bounds and supporting proofs in Section 4.2 and Appendices E.1/H, plus the non-periodic construction in Appendix G. It makes logarithmic factors explicit and supplies an in-document derivative-inequality proof. It also reverses the mollifier exponent's sign between v1 Equation (47) and v2 Equation (50), contradicting its asserted smoothness.

C1.justification: V2 adds a claimed first second-order finite-sample analysis and conditional generalization to non-periodic functions to its contributions. The existing claims of optimal uniform function/derivative estimation and optimal prediction-time memory remain.

C2.justification: The periodicity discussion changes from an informal boundary-subtraction argument to an explicit requirement for outside-domain queries. V2 also explains variance-sensitive guarantees, the logarithmic penalty of using the Dirichlet kernel, and mixed smoothness as a possible response to high-dimensional limitations. Empirical interpretations remain stable.

D1.justification: Section 7 removes v1's description of loading the .wav recording with librosa into a one-dimensional NumPy array. This slightly reduces preprocessing information; neither version provides corresponding new code-access or hardware details.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning around plug-in derivative estimation, finite differences, splines and RKHS methods. It adds detailed comparisons with Liu and Li (2023) and Maran and Szepesvari (2025), replacing the earlier brief Gaussian-process/Matern discussion and broadening the second-order and bandit literature context.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the title, abstract, substantial introductory material and conclusion, adds an explicit contributions subsection and future-work discussion, and reorganizes related work. PADUA becomes DUPA, and several section headings and design terminology change.

P2.justification: A document-wide template change alters typography, margins, text width and figure sizing/placement. Table 1 gains a kernel-ridge-regression row, and Appendix G adds Algorithm 2. The existing plots retain their content, with updated algorithm legends.

improvement.justification: The expanded positioning, explicit rates and proposed theoretical extensions improve scope and explanation, but new correctness problems prevent a reliable net judgment. V2 Equation (50) reverses the previously correct mollifier exponent, making it diverge at the boundary and undermining the lower-bound and cutoff constructions as written. Algorithm 2 also applies the negative perturbation's cutoff to the positive query, inconsistent with estimating fH. These defects affect central supporting arguments, so the added theoretical breadth cannot confidently be credited as an overall quality improvement.
